title: The Shinnecock Indians (1950): Book Guide
summary: A chapter-by-chapter guide to Lois Marie Hunter’s 1950 Shinnecock-authored community history, connecting the book to related people, places, events, and research topics.
content:
Lois Marie Hunter’s The Shinnecock Indians is a Shinnecock-authored community history published by Buys Bros. in 1950. Hunter organized documentary history, church records, family memory, biography, work, education, and community continuity into a short book. This guide accounts for the complete volume and connects each section to related On This Site people, places, and topics.

The page references below use the 46-page scanned PDF. Hunter’s language and conclusions belong to their 1950 setting. Population figures, individual service records, voyage details, and other claims that require newer evidence are presented as her account rather than as current fact.

Front matter and Hunter’s purpose — PDF pp. 1–6

The cover, frontispiece, title page, copyright, dedication, introduction, and contents establish Hunter’s authorship and purpose. She dedicated the book to Abigail Fithian Halsey and described the project as a walk through ancestral ground and knowledge carried by Shinnecock people. See Lois “Princess Nowedonah” Hunter and Wickham Cuffee.

The Tribe — PDF pp. 7–8

Hunter opens with Shinnecock homeland, community continuity, reservation history, population, and archaeology as understood in 1950. The section is useful as a period account, while current population and archaeological interpretation require current sources and Shinnecock authority. See the Shinnecock Indian Reservation.

Contact, land, and foodways — PDF pp. 9–10

“Red Men Meet the Whites” brings together Conscience Point, Nowedonah, colonial land transactions, agriculture, and food. The land narrative connects to Conscience Point. Food traditions connect to Food and women’s plant knowledge connects to Native Plants; historical remedies are not presented as medical guidance.

Leaders and early ministers — PDF pp. 11–17

Hunter’s chapters on Indian leaders, the Rev. Peter John, the Rev. Azariah Horton, the Rev. Paul Cuffee, and the Rev. Samson Occom place leadership, literacy, Christianity, diplomacy, and education in a connected regional history. Related biographies include Cockenoe, Peter John Cuffee, Rev. Paul Cuffee, and Samson Occom. Hunter’s Azariah Horton account is now incorporated with critical source context in Indian Missions on Long Island.

The old and new churches — PDF pp. 18–22

Hunter records traditions about the old Shinnecock church, the Canoe Place chapel, community worship, the 1938 hurricane, rebuilding, and the dedication of the new sanctuary on September 3, 1939. These chapters connect to the Little Church, Rev. Paul Cuffee Gravesite, and Shinnecock Presbyterian Church. Traditions are identified as Hunter’s account where documentary sources differ.

Shinnecock whalers — PDF pp. 23–24

The whaling chapter presents maritime skill through Shinnecock memory, including dangerous work, navigation, named whalers, the ship Amethyst, and Wickham Cuffee’s ability to read wind and water. It connects to Whaling and Wickham Cuffee. Voyage details that have not been independently confirmed remain attributed to Hunter.

Women, family, education, and survival — PDF pp. 25–27

Hunter used the period title “Only a Squaw” for a chapter that insists on Shinnecock women’s intelligence, labor, care, teaching, family endurance, and public contribution. Its biographies include Rebecca Bunn Kellis, remembered as Aunt Becky, and Mary Emma Cuffee Bunn. See Mary Rebecca Bunn, Mary Emma Cuffee Bunn, Food, and Slavery. Medical preparations in the chapter are historical material, not present-day health advice.

Wreck of the Circassian — PDF pp. 27–28

Hunter’s account preserves the names and community memory of ten Shinnecock men lost after the Circassian broke apart on December 30, 1876. The ship first struck the bar on December 11; distinguishing those dates resolves a conflict in some retellings. See Circassian Shipwreck. Burial-location details are not repeated here.

The Shinnecock School — PDF pp. 29–30

The school chapter records education on the reservation, teachers, changing buildings, and the school as Hunter knew it. Later source checking distinguishes the 1874 fire from the replacement building opened in 1875. The history is connected to Education at Shinnecock and the Shinnecock Indian Reservation without creating a precise school map point.

Trustees of the Tribe — PDF pp. 31–33

Hunter describes the three-man trustee system, elections, lease income, records, clerks, and governance as they operated in 1950. It is a historical snapshot, not a description of present governance. See Tribal Trustees for later political change and contemporary context.

Wickham Cuffee — PDF pp. 33–34

Hunter’s grandfather appears as a whaler, navigator, basketmaker, farmer, elder, and source of family memory. Her biography connects personal knowledge to broader Shinnecock continuity. See Wickham Cuffee.

Thomas Clay Ogburn and Raymond Hastings Case — PDF pp. 35–39

These ministerial chapters describe church leadership, community relationships, fundraising, and change during the early twentieth century. Ogburn’s ministry is incorporated as Hunter’s attributed account. Hunter’s 1936 powwow-fundraiser claim is preserved in the Powwow and church histories as an explicit chronology conflict rather than a settled origin date. See the Shinnecock Presbyterian Church and Shinnecock Powwow Grounds.

Herbert E. Moyer and rebuilding — PDF pp. 40–41

Hunter credits the Rev. Herbert E. Moyer’s church work and records the September 21, 1938 hurricane damage that led to rebuilding. This section supports the church history and its existing 1938–1939 Historic Moment. See the Shinnecock Presbyterian Church.

The cemetery — PDF pp. 41–42

Hunter discusses memorial care, people buried near the church, and an older burial place. This guide retains only broad community-remembrance context. It does not publish directions or descriptive location details for the older burial ground.

War effort — PDF pp. 43–44

Hunter records Shinnecock participation in American wars and names people associated with military service. The chapter now supports Shinnecock Veterans and Wartime Service. Hunter’s honor roll is treated as a 1950 community record while individual units, dates, and duties remain subject to service-record verification.

Conclusion — PDF pp. 45–46

Hunter closes by rejecting disappearance narratives and emphasizing continuing Shinnecock life. She also preserves family remembrance about Wickham Cuffee, older homes, and language. These claims are presented as Hunter’s community and family memory. See Lois Hunter, Wickham Cuffee, and the Shinnecock Indian Reservation.

Illustrations and captions — PDF pp. 2–45

The volume includes portraits, drawings, church imagery, a school image, maritime scenes, and memorial imagery. Their subjects and captions are part of the research record. The drawing on PDF p. 3 (book p. IV) is identified by the facing-page caption on PDF p. 2 (book p. III) as Wickham Cuffee and appears with source credit in the Wickham Cuffee article. Other scans remain in the private media inventory until their identity, destination, and reuse status are reviewed.

Source

Lois Marie Hunter, The Shinnecock Indians (Buys Bros., 1950). Page references above refer to the 46-page scanned PDF.
activity_update_summary: Connected Hunter's foodways, plant knowledge, education, governance, ministry, powwow, and wartime-service chapters to their permanent articles and listings.
